oil.summary: Crude markets surged Thursday, with Brent settling above $112/bbl (+3.44% on the day, +9.20% on the month) and WTI clearing $99/bbl, driven squarely by Middle East escalation. Iran's IRGC Navy claimed seven vessels—including oil tankers—were struck in the Persian Gulf, compounding earlier Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure and tanker damage reported earlier in the week. Strait of Hormuz closure risk is the dominant fear premium in the market. Citi, which had called for $60 oil, now acknowledges more upside risk. A partial offset came from the Trump administration's temporary waiver on select Russian oil sanctions, which briefly weighed on futures mid-week but failed to cap the geopolitical bid. Product markets diverged sharply: RBOB gasoline fell 1.18% on the day and is down 14% on the month, while heating oil also slipped, suggesting demand-side softness at the refined-products level despite surging crude.
drivers: IRGC claims seven ships struck in Persian Gulf, escalating Strait of Hormuz closure risk and driving a sharp geopolitical risk premium into crude
Houthi attacks on Saudi energy sites and ongoing US-Iran conflict sustaining regional supply-disruption fears
Trump administration's temporary waiver on Russian oil sanctions providing partial bearish offset but insufficient to reverse the geopolitical bid

gas.summary: European and US gas markets diverged sharply Thursday. TTF rose 3.29% on the day to 90.3 €/MWh—a 25.4% monthly gain—as Middle East escalation stoked broader energy supply anxiety and the EU reaffirmed sanctions on Russian LNG will remain in place until the war ends, per von der Leyen. A headline noting TTF near €90/MWh, equivalent to roughly $29.50/MMBtu, underscores the continued trans-Atlantic price dislocation. Ofgem's approval of a deal to preserve UK gas import capacity from European connectors signals regulatory awareness of tightening supply flexibility. The Jackdaw North Sea field approval offers a longer-term incremental supply story but provides no near-term relief. Henry Hub, by contrast, softened to $2.82/MMBtu, down 12.86% on the week, reflecting looser domestic US fundamentals disconnected from the geopolitical shock hitting Europe.
drivers: EU reaffirms Russian LNG sanctions remain in force, keeping European supply structurally constrained and supporting TTF at elevated levels
Middle East escalation and Strait of Hormuz risk driving broad European energy risk premium, lifting TTF 25% over the past month
Henry Hub down sharply week-on-week, highlighting persistent US-Europe price divergence driven by differing supply fundamentals

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged up modestly, gaining 0.93% to $82.26/EUA on the day, with the monthly move essentially flat (+0.65%), suggesting carbon markets are not yet pricing a dramatic demand-destruction or fuel-switching signal from surging energy costs. The backdrop is nonetheless complex: TTF at 90.3 €/MWh continues to pressure gas-fired power economics across Europe, while record fuel prices are reported to be accelerating EV adoption and suppressing conventional vehicle registrations—a structural demand-side shift. In India, the picture is one of stress on multiple fronts: grid and transmission constraints forced curtailment of 118.6 GW of solar and wind capacity in September, while the government is simultaneously ramping coal supply to power plants to avert a power crisis. Carbon market headline flow is thin today; EUA price action appears to be drifting rather than reacting decisively to the macro energy shock.
drivers: TTF at 90.3 €/MWh sustaining pressure on European gas-fired power generation economics, though EUAs are not yet reflecting a strong fuel-switching signal
India curtailed 118.6 GW of renewables in September due to grid and transmission constraints, forcing increased reliance on coal for power supply
Record European fuel prices reported to be accelerating EV adoption, a longer-term demand-side shift with limited immediate carbon price impact
